content_voiceover: This slide walks through the general treatment framework for bone sarcoma, which applies to both Ewing sarcoma and osteosarcoma with some key differences. Treatment starts with preoperative, or neoadjuvant, chemotherapy to shrink the tumor before surgery. Surgery follows, and limb-sparing resection is now possible in about ninety percent of cases, sparing patients from amputation. A critical step at surgery is assessing the histopathologic response to that preoperative chemotherapy, meaning how much viable tumor remains, because this response grade is one of the strongest predictors of outcome and can guide whether postoperative chemotherapy needs to be intensified. After surgery, postoperative chemotherapy continues to eliminate micrometastatic disease. Radiation therapy is where the two tumor types really diverge, radiation is used for Ewing sarcoma in specific situations, large tumors, pelvic primaries, and cases with close surgical margins, because Ewing sarcoma is fairly radiosensitive. Osteosarcoma, on the other hand, is relatively radiation-resistant, so radiation plays essentially no role in its management, and local control depends almost entirely on complete surgical resection.
keypoints: Sequence: neoadjuvant chemo, then surgery, then adjuvant chemo
Limb-sparing surgery achievable in about 90% of cases
Histopathologic response to preop chemo predicts prognosis
Radiation used for Ewing sarcoma with large, pelvic, or close-margin tumors
Osteosarcoma is relatively radioresistant, so surgery drives local control
